title: Naive Bayes
interviewAnswer: Naive Bayes applies Bayes rule while assuming features are conditionally independent given the class. Despite the strong assumption, it can work surprisingly well for text and sparse features.
why: Naive Bayes connects Bayes rule, conditional independence and simple high-dimensional classifiers.
intuition: Estimate how likely each feature is under each class, multiply those pieces with the class prior, and choose the class with the largest posterior score.
deepDive: The “naive” assumption is conditional independence of features given the class. Despite being unrealistic, it can work well when likelihood ratios still rank classes effectively, especially for text. Gaussian, Multinomial and Bernoulli variants use different feature likelihoods. Computation uses log probabilities to avoid underflow and turn products into sums.
math:
P(y|x) ∝ P(y) Π_j P(x_j|y)
log score = log P(y)+Σ_j log P(x_j|y)
workedExample: Multinomial Naive Bayes can classify documents from token counts because word evidence combines efficiently even with thousands of sparse features.
commonMistakes: Saying features must be marginally independent.
Multiplying tiny probabilities directly instead of using logs.
Choosing Gaussian NB for arbitrary count data without modeling logic.
followUps: Why can Naive Bayes work despite the independence assumption?
production: Naive Bayes is fast and useful as a sparse baseline; calibration and distribution shift should still be checked.
